items.title: I can identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables in an experiment
items.what: The independent variable is deliberately changed by the experimenter. The dependent variable is what is measured in response. Controlled variables are everything else that is kept constant to prevent them from influencing the results.
items.why: Clearly identifying these three variable types is essential for designing a valid experiment. If controlled variables are not held constant, it becomes impossible to know whether changes in the dependent variable are caused by the independent variable.
items.example: In an experiment testing how the angle of a ramp affects the time a ball takes to reach the bottom: the angle is the independent variable, the time is the dependent variable, and the length of the ramp and the size of the ball are controlled variables.

subtopic.name: Variables, Data and the Scientific Method
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to identify and classify variables in an experiment, distinguish between types of data, and apply the five steps of the scientific method. It also introduces the distinction between scientific hypotheses, laws, models and theories.
subtopic.why: Understanding variable types and the scientific method is foundational to designing valid experiments and interpreting results correctly. Without clearly defined variables, it is impossible to establish a reliable cause-and-effect relationship.

items.title: I can distinguish between primary and secondary data
items.what: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher conducting the experiment. Secondary data is obtained from existing sources such as published studies, databases or other researchers' experiments.
items.why: Knowing the origin of data matters for evaluating its reliability and applicability. Primary data is directly tied to the specific conditions of your investigation, while secondary data may have been collected under different conditions.
items.example: A student who measures the extension of a spring themselves is collecting primary data. If they instead use values from a published textbook table, they are using secondary data.

subtopic.why: Understanding variable types and the scientific method is foundational to designing valid experiments and interpreting results correctly. Without clearly defined variables, it is impossible to establish a reliable cause-and-effect relationship.

items.title: I can distinguish between quantitative and qualitative data
items.what: Quantitative data is expressed as a numerical value, while qualitative data is expressed using non-numerical descriptions. Both types can be either primary or secondary.
items.why: Correctly classifying data as quantitative or qualitative determines how it can be analysed and communicated. Quantitative data allows for mathematical analysis, while qualitative data captures observations that cannot be reduced to numbers.
items.example: Recording the extension of a spring as 4.3 cm is quantitative data. Recording that a surface appeared rough or smooth is qualitative data.

items.title: I can write a well-structured hypothesis for an experiment
items.what: A hypothesis is a testable prediction that describes the expected relationship between the independent and dependent variables. A useful structure is: 'It is predicted that [increasing/decreasing] [independent variable] will [increase/decrease] [dependent variable] because [reason].'
items.why: A clearly written hypothesis gives direction to the experiment and provides a specific claim that the results can either support or fail to support. Vague or untestable hypotheses cannot be meaningfully evaluated.
items.example: For an experiment on bouncing balls: 'It is predicted that increasing the height from which a rubber ball is dropped will increase the height of the initial bounce, because a greater drop height means the ball has more gravitational potential energy to convert to kinetic energy on impact.'

subtopic.why: Understanding variable types and the scientific method is foundational to designing valid experiments and interpreting results correctly. Without clearly defined variables, it is impossible to establish a reliable cause-and-effect relationship.

items.title: I can describe the five steps of the scientific method and explain the purpose of each
items.what: The scientific method involves: (1) observing and questioning a phenomenon, (2) formulating an aim and hypothesis, (3) designing and conducting an experiment, (4) analysing data and drawing conclusions, and (5) sharing results with the broader scientific community.
items.why: Following the scientific method systematically reduces the chance of reaching incorrect conclusions. Each step builds on the previous one and the process of sharing and replication is what builds confidence in scientific knowledge over time.
items.example: A student notices a pendulum swings more slowly when made longer, forms a hypothesis, measures the period at five different lengths, plots the data and draws a conclusion, then writes up their findings for a scientific poster.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how to identify and classify variables in an experiment, distinguish between types of data, and apply the five steps of the scientific method. It also introduces the distinction between scientific hypotheses, laws, models and theories.
subtopic.why: Understanding variable types and the scientific method is foundational to designing valid experiments and interpreting results correctly. Without clearly defined variables, it is impossible to establish a reliable cause-and-effect relationship.

items.title: I can distinguish between a scientific hypothesis, theory, model and law
items.what: A hypothesis is an initial testable prediction. A theory is a well-tested explanation that accounts for observations and has withstood repeated attempts at disproof. A law is a concise statement of what happens in a phenomenon. A model is a simplified representation of a physical process that may be incomplete.
items.why: These terms are used precisely in science and have different levels of evidential support. Confusing them — particularly calling a hypothesis a theory — misrepresents how confident the scientific community is in an explanation.
items.example: Newton's first law of motion is a law — it states what happens (objects in motion stay in motion unless acted upon). The kinetic theory of matter is a theory — it explains why gases expand. The wave model of light is a model — it is useful but incomplete.

items.title: I can identify and use base SI units for common physical quantities
items.what: The seven base SI units include the metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, ampere (A) for electric current, and kelvin (K) for temperature. All other units are derived from combinations of these.
items.why: Most physics formulas require quantities to be expressed in SI units before substitution. Using non-SI units (such as grams instead of kilograms) will produce incorrect numerical results.
items.example: A problem asking for force in newtons requires mass in kilograms and acceleration in m s⁻². If mass is given in grams, it must be converted to kilograms first: 250 g = 0.250 kg.

subtopic.name: Scientific Conventions: Units and Significant Figures
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the SI unit system including base and derived units, how to use prefixes to express different orders of magnitude, and how to apply significant figure conventions when recording and calculating values. It also addresses the use of scientific notation.
subtopic.why: Consistent use of SI units and significant figures allows scientists to communicate measurements clearly and accurately. Without these conventions, it would be impossible to compare results across experiments or interpret the level of confidence in a measurement.

items.title: I can convert measurements using SI prefixes
items.what: SI prefixes indicate multiplication factors: pico (10⁻¹²), nano (10⁻⁹), micro (10⁻⁶), milli (10⁻³), kilo (10³), mega (10⁶) and giga (10⁹). Converting between prefixes means multiplying or dividing by the appropriate power of ten.
items.why: Scientific measurements span enormous ranges of scale. Prefixes make values easier to write and read, but they must be removed before substituting into formulas to avoid calculation errors.
items.example: Converting 360 nm to metres: 360 nm = 360 × 10⁻⁹ m = 3.60 × 10⁻⁷ m. Converting 23 MΩ to ohms: 23 × 10⁶ = 2.3 × 10⁷ Ω.

subtopic.name: Scientific Conventions: Units and Significant Figures
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the SI unit system including base and derived units, how to use prefixes to express different orders of magnitude, and how to apply significant figure conventions when recording and calculating values. It also addresses the use of scientific notation.
subtopic.why: Consistent use of SI units and significant figures allows scientists to communicate measurements clearly and accurately. Without these conventions, it would be impossible to compare results across experiments or interpret the level of confidence in a measurement.

items.title: I can determine the number of significant figures in a value
items.what: Significant figures include all non-zero digits, zeros between digits, and trailing zeros after a decimal point. Leading zeros are never significant. The number of significant figures indicates how precisely a value is known.
items.why: Expressing a result with too many significant figures implies a level of precision that was not actually achieved. Using too few significant figures loses information about the precision of the measurement.
items.example: The value 0.0302 has three significant figures (the leading zeros are not significant, but the zero between 3 and 2 is). The value 53.00 has four significant figures because the trailing zeros after the decimal place are significant.

subtopic.name: Scientific Conventions: Units and Significant Figures
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the SI unit system including base and derived units, how to use prefixes to express different orders of magnitude, and how to apply significant figure conventions when recording and calculating values. It also addresses the use of scientific notation.
subtopic.why: Consistent use of SI units and significant figures allows scientists to communicate measurements clearly and accurately. Without these conventions, it would be impossible to compare results across experiments or interpret the level of confidence in a measurement.

items.title: I can apply significant figure rules when performing calculations
items.what: When multiplying or dividing, the answer should have the same number of significant figures as the least precise input value. When adding or subtracting, the answer should have the same number of decimal places as the input with the fewest decimal places.
items.why: These rules ensure the calculated result does not express more confidence than is justified by the input data. Rounding should only be applied to the final answer, not to intermediate steps, to avoid compounding rounding errors.
items.example: For 34.477 × 2.31: the answer is limited to 3 significant figures (from 2.31), giving 79.6. For 34.477 + 2.31: the answer is limited to 2 decimal places (from 2.31), giving 36.79.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the SI unit system including base and derived units, how to use prefixes to express different orders of magnitude, and how to apply significant figure conventions when recording and calculating values. It also addresses the use of scientific notation.
subtopic.why: Consistent use of SI units and significant figures allows scientists to communicate measurements clearly and accurately. Without these conventions, it would be impossible to compare results across experiments or interpret the level of confidence in a measurement.

items.title: I can write values in correct scientific notation
items.what: Scientific notation expresses a number as m × 10ⁿ, where m is a value with an absolute value between 1 and 10, and n is an integer. All digits in m are significant. Scientific notation is used to express very large or very small numbers, and to communicate precision clearly.
items.why: Scientific notation prevents ambiguity about significant figures and makes very large or small numbers easier to read and compare. For example, writing 2.0 × 10¹ m makes it clear there are two significant figures, whereas writing 20 m does not.
items.example: 63 700 written to 2 significant figures is 6.4 × 10⁴. The value 0.00034 written in scientific notation is 3.4 × 10⁻⁴. The value 0.0125 to 2 significant figures is 1.3 × 10⁻².

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the SI unit system including base and derived units, how to use prefixes to express different orders of magnitude, and how to apply significant figure conventions when recording and calculating values. It also addresses the use of scientific notation.
subtopic.why: Consistent use of SI units and significant figures allows scientists to communicate measurements clearly and accurately. Without these conventions, it would be impossible to compare results across experiments or interpret the level of confidence in a measurement.

items.title: I can distinguish between accuracy and precision in a set of measurements
items.what: Precision describes how closely repeated measurements agree with each other — a precise set has a small spread. Accuracy describes how closely the average of measurements agrees with the true value. A set can be precise but inaccurate, or accurate but imprecise.
items.why: These two qualities address different problems: imprecision is linked to random error, while inaccuracy is often linked to systematic error. Identifying which quality is poor helps diagnose the correct source of the problem.
items.example: If a student repeatedly measures a wire as 12.3 cm, 12.4 cm and 12.3 cm, but the true length is 15.0 cm, the data is precise (small spread) but inaccurate (far from the true value). This pattern is typical of a systematic error.

subtopic.name: Collecting Data: Accuracy, Precision and Error
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers precision, accuracy, resolution, and the three types of experimental error: systematic, random and personal. It also introduces the concept of uncertainty and how it is expressed and interpreted.
subtopic.why: Understanding how errors arise and how they affect data quality is essential for evaluating experimental results. Identifying sources of error allows scientists to improve their methods and appropriately qualify their conclusions.

items.title: I can define resolution and explain how it affects uncertainty
items.what: Resolution is the smallest detectable change in a measuring instrument. A higher-resolution instrument can detect smaller differences. For analogue instruments, uncertainty is typically taken as half the smallest scale division.
items.why: The resolution of a measuring instrument sets a lower limit on how small the uncertainty in a measurement can be. Choosing an instrument with higher resolution directly reduces measurement uncertainty.
items.example: A ruler marked in millimetres has a resolution of 1 mm, giving an uncertainty of ±0.5 mm. A ruler marked only in centimetres has a resolution of 1 cm and a larger uncertainty of ±0.5 cm.

subtopic.name: Collecting Data: Accuracy, Precision and Error
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers precision, accuracy, resolution, and the three types of experimental error: systematic, random and personal. It also introduces the concept of uncertainty and how it is expressed and interpreted.
subtopic.why: Understanding how errors arise and how they affect data quality is essential for evaluating experimental results. Identifying sources of error allows scientists to improve their methods and appropriately qualify their conclusions.

items.title: I can identify and describe systematic error and explain how it affects data
items.what: Systematic error is a consistent, repeatable deviation of measured values from the true value. It affects all data points in the same direction and by approximately the same amount. Common causes include uncalibrated equipment or parallax error.
items.why: Systematic error cannot be reduced by averaging repeated measurements, since every measurement is shifted in the same direction. It must be addressed by improving the experimental design or recalibrating equipment.
items.example: If a set of scales reads 5 g too high for every object weighed because it was not zeroed before use, all measurements will be shifted upward by 5 g. This is a systematic error caused by a calibration problem.

subtopic.name: Collecting Data: Accuracy, Precision and Error
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers precision, accuracy, resolution, and the three types of experimental error: systematic, random and personal. It also introduces the concept of uncertainty and how it is expressed and interpreted.
subtopic.why: Understanding how errors arise and how they affect data quality is essential for evaluating experimental results. Identifying sources of error allows scientists to improve their methods and appropriately qualify their conclusions.

items.title: I can identify and describe random error and explain how it can be reduced
items.what: Random error is the unpredictable variation in measurements caused by uncontrolled factors such as slight differences in conditions between trials or difficulty reading an analogue scale. It causes data points to scatter around the true value.
items.why: Unlike systematic error, random error can be reduced by taking more measurements and averaging them. The more measurements taken, the closer the average is likely to be to the true value.
items.example: When timing how long a ball takes to roll down a ramp, a student's reaction time introduces random error. Taking five measurements and averaging them reduces the effect of any single timing mistake.

subtopic.name: Collecting Data: Accuracy, Precision and Error
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers precision, accuracy, resolution, and the three types of experimental error: systematic, random and personal. It also introduces the concept of uncertainty and how it is expressed and interpreted.
subtopic.why: Understanding how errors arise and how they affect data quality is essential for evaluating experimental results. Identifying sources of error allows scientists to improve their methods and appropriately qualify their conclusions.

items.title: I can identify personal error and explain why it invalidates data
items.what: Personal error is a mistake in the execution or analysis of an experiment caused by a lack of care. Examples include misreading a scale, recording the wrong value, or deliberately selecting data that fits the expected result.
items.why: Personal errors are not genuine measurement limitations — they are avoidable mistakes. Data affected by personal error should not be included in the analysis, and the error should be noted in the logbook.
items.example: A student reads a thermometer while looking at it from the side rather than straight on, and records 23°C instead of the correct 21°C. This is a personal error caused by failing to read the instrument correctly.

subtopic.why: Understanding how errors arise and how they affect data quality is essential for evaluating experimental results. Identifying sources of error allows scientists to improve their methods and appropriately qualify their conclusions.

items.title: I can express and interpret uncertainty in measurements
items.what: Uncertainty is expressed in the form: measured value ± uncertainty. It indicates the range within which the true value is expected to lie. Uncertainty bars on a graph convey the same information visually for each data point.
items.why: Expressing uncertainty quantifies the reliability of a measurement and prevents overconfident claims. All measurements carry some uncertainty, and ignoring this can lead to incorrect conclusions about whether results match theoretical predictions.
items.example: A measurement recorded as 35 ± 1 mm means the true value is expected to lie somewhere between 34 mm and 36 mm. On a graph, a vertical uncertainty bar of ±1 mm is drawn above and below the data point.

items.title: I can explain what makes an experiment valid
items.what: A valid experiment is one that actually measures what it intends to measure. Validity requires only one independent variable to be changed at a time, appropriate controlled variables, suitable equipment, and unbiased data collection and analysis.
items.why: If an experiment is not valid, the results cannot be used to draw meaningful conclusions about the relationship being investigated. Invalid experiments waste time and resources, and can lead to incorrect or misleading findings.
items.example: An experiment testing how light intensity affects photocurrent is invalid if the experimenter also changes the colour (wavelength) of the light between trials, because this introduces a second independent variable.

subtopic.name: Validity, Repeatability, Reproducibility and Logbooks
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what makes an experiment valid, the difference between repeatability and reproducibility, and the purpose and contents of an experimental logbook. These concepts link experimental design to the quality and trustworthiness of the results obtained.
subtopic.why: Even a carefully executed experiment can produce meaningless data if the design is flawed or if the method cannot be replicated. Understanding validity, repeatability and reproducibility is what separates reliable science from one-off results that cannot be trusted.

items.title: I can distinguish between repeatability and reproducibility
items.what: Repeatability refers to how closely results agree when the same experimenter repeats the same experiment under the same conditions. Reproducibility refers to how closely results agree when a different experimenter repeats the experiment, possibly with different equipment.
items.why: Repeatability confirms that the results are consistent within a single experimental context. Reproducibility is a stronger test: it confirms that the findings are not specific to one lab, one set of equipment, or one experimenter's technique.
items.example: If a student measures the same spring constant three times in their own lab and gets consistent results, the experiment is repeatable. If a student at a different school uses their own equipment and gets a similar value, the result is reproducible.

subtopic.name: Validity, Repeatability, Reproducibility and Logbooks
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what makes an experiment valid, the difference between repeatability and reproducibility, and the purpose and contents of an experimental logbook. These concepts link experimental design to the quality and trustworthiness of the results obtained.
subtopic.why: Even a carefully executed experiment can produce meaningless data if the design is flawed or if the method cannot be replicated. Understanding validity, repeatability and reproducibility is what separates reliable science from one-off results that cannot be trusted.

items.title: I can explain the purpose of a logbook and describe what it should contain
items.what: A logbook is a complete, chronological record of an experiment. It should include dates and times of entries, all raw data, the step-by-step method, diagrams of the apparatus, any errors or unexpected events, calculations, and conclusions.
items.why: A logbook authenticates the data generated in an experiment. It allows the experimenter to verify their own results later, enables other researchers to reproduce the work, and provides a transparent record of how and when data was collected.
items.example: If a student records that their voltmeter malfunctioned partway through a trial and was replaced with a different model, this logbook entry allows future experimenters to understand a potential source of inconsistency in the data.

subtopic.name: Validity, Repeatability, Reproducibility and Logbooks
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what makes an experiment valid, the difference between repeatability and reproducibility, and the purpose and contents of an experimental logbook. These concepts link experimental design to the quality and trustworthiness of the results obtained.
subtopic.why: Even a carefully executed experiment can produce meaningless data if the design is flawed or if the method cannot be replicated. Understanding validity, repeatability and reproducibility is what separates reliable science from one-off results that cannot be trusted.

items.title: I can identify actions that would make an experiment invalid
items.what: An experiment becomes invalid when more than one independent variable is changed at once, when controlled variables are allowed to shift during trials, when personal error affects data collection, or when data is selectively reported without acknowledgement.
items.why: Each of these actions breaks the logic of the experiment. If the cause of a change in the dependent variable cannot be isolated to the independent variable, no valid conclusion can be drawn.
items.example: If a student changes both the length and the mass of a pendulum between trials to 'save time', the results cannot tell them which variable is responsible for any change in the period.

subtopic.why: Even a carefully executed experiment can produce meaningless data if the design is flawed or if the method cannot be replicated. Understanding validity, repeatability and reproducibility is what separates reliable science from one-off results that cannot be trusted.

items.title: I can construct a correctly formatted scientific graph from experimental data
items.what: A scientific graph should have the independent variable on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical axis. Both axes must be labelled with the variable name and units. The title should follow the format '[dependent variable] vs. [independent variable]'. The scale should be consistent and spread the data across at least 50% of the graph space.
items.why: Following graphing conventions ensures the graph communicates data clearly and allows the reader to extract values accurately. An inconsistent scale or swapped axes makes the graph misleading or unreadable.
items.example: For an experiment measuring the time for a block to slide down a ramp at various angles, the title would be 'Time for block to slide down ramp vs. ramp angle', with 'Ramp angle (°)' on the horizontal axis and 'Time (s)' on the vertical axis.

subtopic.name: Representing and Analysing Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the conventions for creating scientific graphs, drawing lines of best fit, using uncertainty bars, linearising data, and calculating and interpreting gradients. These skills are used to identify relationships between variables and extract physical meaning from experimental results.
subtopic.why: Representing data graphically allows patterns and relationships to be seen that are not obvious from a table of numbers. Calculating the gradient of a linearised graph is one of the most powerful tools for connecting experimental data to physical equations.

items.title: I can add uncertainty bars to a graph and explain what they represent
items.what: Uncertainty bars are drawn as lines extending above and below (vertical) or left and right (horizontal) of each data point, with end caps. Their length represents the magnitude of the uncertainty. Together, vertical and horizontal uncertainty bars define a rectangular region within which the true value is expected to lie.
items.why: Uncertainty bars make the reliability of each data point visible. They also determine whether a straight line of best fit is valid — the line must pass through the uncertainty bar region of every data point.
items.example: If the time measurement has an uncertainty of ±0.2 s, the vertical uncertainty bar for a data point at (30°, 2.0 s) would extend from 1.8 s to 2.2 s on the vertical axis.

subtopic.name: Representing and Analysing Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the conventions for creating scientific graphs, drawing lines of best fit, using uncertainty bars, linearising data, and calculating and interpreting gradients. These skills are used to identify relationships between variables and extract physical meaning from experimental results.
subtopic.why: Representing data graphically allows patterns and relationships to be seen that are not obvious from a table of numbers. Calculating the gradient of a linearised graph is one of the most powerful tools for connecting experimental data to physical equations.

items.title: I can draw a valid straight line or curved line of best fit
items.what: A line of best fit must pass through the uncertainty bar region of every data point. It should be smooth and should not be forced to pass through the origin or any specific data point. If no straight line can pass through all uncertainty bars, a curved line of best fit must be used instead.
items.why: The line of best fit represents the underlying trend in the data and smooths out random error. Forcing it through the origin or a specific point introduces bias and can lead to an incorrect physical interpretation.
items.example: If a curved data set like the time-vs-angle graph cannot be described by a single straight line passing through all uncertainty bars, a smooth curve must be drawn instead of a straight line.

subtopic.name: Representing and Analysing Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the conventions for creating scientific graphs, drawing lines of best fit, using uncertainty bars, linearising data, and calculating and interpreting gradients. These skills are used to identify relationships between variables and extract physical meaning from experimental results.
subtopic.why: Representing data graphically allows patterns and relationships to be seen that are not obvious from a table of numbers. Calculating the gradient of a linearised graph is one of the most powerful tools for connecting experimental data to physical equations.

items.title: I can linearise data by transforming variables and explain why this is done
items.what: Linearising means transforming one or both variables so that a graph of the transformed data produces a straight line. Common transformations include squaring the variable (for parabolic relationships), taking the square root (for square root relationships), or taking the reciprocal (for hyperbolic relationships).
items.why: A straight-line graph is far easier to analyse than a curve. Once data is linearised, the gradient and intercept of the straight line can be used to determine physical constants and verify mathematical relationships.
items.example: If distance d is proportional to time squared t² (as in free fall from rest), plotting d vs. t gives a curve. Plotting d vs. t² gives a straight line through the origin, confirming the proportional relationship d ∝ t².

subtopic.name: Representing and Analysing Data
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the conventions for creating scientific graphs, drawing lines of best fit, using uncertainty bars, linearising data, and calculating and interpreting gradients. These skills are used to identify relationships between variables and extract physical meaning from experimental results.
subtopic.why: Representing data graphically allows patterns and relationships to be seen that are not obvious from a table of numbers. Calculating the gradient of a linearised graph is one of the most powerful tools for connecting experimental data to physical equations.

items.title: I can calculate the gradient of a straight line of best fit correctly
items.what: The gradient is calculated using two points on the line of best fit (not data points): gradient = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁). The two points should be chosen far apart on the line to reduce the effect of reading errors. Units of the gradient are the units of the vertical axis divided by the units of the horizontal axis.
items.why: Using points close together amplifies the effect of any small error in reading the graph, making the gradient less accurate. The gradient has physical meaning — it represents the rate of change of the dependent variable with respect to the independent variable.
items.example: On a speed vs. time graph, choosing (1.0 s, 9.8 m s⁻¹) and (5.0 s, 49.0 m s⁻¹): gradient = (49.0 − 9.8) / (5.0 − 1.0) = 39.2 / 4.0 = 9.8 m s⁻², which is the acceleration due to gravity.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the conventions for creating scientific graphs, drawing lines of best fit, using uncertainty bars, linearising data, and calculating and interpreting gradients. These skills are used to identify relationships between variables and extract physical meaning from experimental results.
subtopic.why: Representing data graphically allows patterns and relationships to be seen that are not obvious from a table of numbers. Calculating the gradient of a linearised graph is one of the most powerful tools for connecting experimental data to physical equations.

items.title: I can interpret the physical meaning of a gradient by linking it to a physics equation
items.what: The physical meaning of a gradient is found by comparing the axes of the graph to a known physics equation. If the equation is y = mx + c, the gradient m equals whatever quantity is multiplied by x in the equation.
items.why: This is one of the most commonly tested skills in VCE Physics examinations. The gradient of a linearised graph can be used to calculate an experimental value for a physical constant, which can then be compared to the accepted theoretical value.
items.example: If a graph of ΔT vs. Q is plotted for an object being heated, and the known equation is ΔT = Q/(mc), then the gradient = 1/(mc). If the gradient is 4.5 × 10⁻³ °C J⁻¹ and m = 2.0 kg, then c = 1/(2.0 × 4.5 × 10⁻³) ≈ 110 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹.

items.title: I can write a title for a scientific investigation as a research question
items.what: The title of a scientific poster should be posed as a research question that clearly identifies the independent and dependent variables of the investigation.
items.why: Framing the title as a research question immediately communicates what the investigation is testing. It also sets up the hypothesis and aim that follow in the introduction.
items.example: A suitable title for an experiment about ball bounce height is: 'How does the height from which a rubber ball is dropped affect the maximum height of its initial bounce?'

subtopic.name: Communicating Findings: Scientific Posters
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structure and content requirements of a scientific poster as specified by VCAA. It addresses each section — title, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references — and explains what belongs in each.
subtopic.why: Communicating findings clearly and completely is an essential part of the scientific method. A well-constructed poster allows others to evaluate and replicate the investigation, which is fundamental to the process of building scientific knowledge.

items.title: I can write an introduction that includes background theory, key definitions, an aim and a hypothesis
items.what: The introduction should present reliable background information relevant to the investigation, define key terms, state relevant formulas, and clearly present the experimental aim and hypothesis.
items.why: The introduction gives the reader the theoretical context needed to evaluate the investigation. Without it, the significance of the results and their connection to underlying physics cannot be understood.
items.example: An investigation into ramp angle and ball travel time would include the formula F = mg sin(θ) in the introduction, with an explanation of how a steeper angle increases the net force on the ball and therefore its acceleration.

subtopic.name: Communicating Findings: Scientific Posters
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structure and content requirements of a scientific poster as specified by VCAA. It addresses each section — title, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references — and explains what belongs in each.
subtopic.why: Communicating findings clearly and completely is an essential part of the scientific method. A well-constructed poster allows others to evaluate and replicate the investigation, which is fundamental to the process of building scientific knowledge.

items.title: I can write a methodology that includes materials, a labelled diagram and a reproducible step-by-step procedure
items.what: The methodology must list specific materials, include a clearly labelled diagram or photograph of the experimental setup, and provide a numbered step-by-step procedure written in the third person (avoiding 'I' or 'we').
items.why: A clear methodology allows other researchers to replicate the investigation exactly. Writing in the third person and avoiding first-person language is standard scientific convention and ensures the method reads as a general procedure rather than a personal account.
items.example: Instead of writing 'I tilted the ramp to 30°', write 'Adjust the ramp until it makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal surface, as measured using a protractor.'

subtopic.why: Communicating findings clearly and completely is an essential part of the scientific method. A well-constructed poster allows others to evaluate and replicate the investigation, which is fundamental to the process of building scientific knowledge.

items.title: I can present results in an appropriate format and explain whether they support the hypothesis
items.what: The results section presents raw data in a table or graph (not both, to avoid redundancy), includes a brief explanation of key features, and states whether the data appears to support or not support the hypothesis.
items.why: The results section should present the data clearly without interpretation. A brief statement about whether the data aligns with the hypothesis prepares the reader for the more detailed analysis in the discussion.
items.example: A graph showing that ball travel time decreases as ramp angle increases, followed by the statement: 'The results appear to support the hypothesis, as each increase in angle corresponded to a decrease in travel time.'

subtopic.why: Communicating findings clearly and completely is an essential part of the scientific method. A well-constructed poster allows others to evaluate and replicate the investigation, which is fundamental to the process of building scientific knowledge.

items.title: I can write a discussion that analyses results, identifies sources of error and links findings to the aim
items.what: The discussion should evaluate how well the results support the hypothesis, compare results to theoretical predictions, identify possible sources of error and suggest how they could be minimised, acknowledge any outliers, and link the findings back to the aim.
items.why: The discussion is where the investigation is evaluated critically. It moves beyond describing results to explaining them in terms of the underlying physics and acknowledging the limitations of the approach taken.
items.example: A discussion might note that experimental times for a ball rolling down a ramp were consistently longer than those predicted theoretically, and identify friction as the likely cause of this systematic discrepancy.

subtopic.name: Communicating Findings: Scientific Posters
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structure and content requirements of a scientific poster as specified by VCAA. It addresses each section — title, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references — and explains what belongs in each.
subtopic.why: Communicating findings clearly and completely is an essential part of the scientific method. A well-constructed poster allows others to evaluate and replicate the investigation, which is fundamental to the process of building scientific knowledge.

items.title: I can write a conclusion that states the main finding, uses appropriate language and identifies limitations
items.what: A conclusion should state the main finding of the investigation, specify whether the data supports or did not support the hypothesis using language such as 'supports', 'partially supports' or 'does not support', and identify limitations and possible improvements. The words 'proved' and 'disproved' must not be used.
items.why: Science never proves anything with absolute certainty. Using the word 'proved' misrepresents the nature of scientific evidence. A conclusion also builds scientific value by identifying what would make the investigation stronger.
items.example: A correct conclusion might read: 'The results support the hypothesis that increasing the angle of inclination reduces the time for the ball to reach the bottom of the ramp. The investigation was limited by the small number of angles tested; future investigations could use a wider range and finer angle increments.'

items.title: I can acknowledge references and sources appropriately in a scientific poster
items.what: Any information, data or ideas used from external sources must be acknowledged in a references and acknowledgements section using a standard referencing style.
items.why: Referencing gives credit to original authors, allows readers to verify the background information presented, and is an ethical requirement in scientific communication.
items.example: Background information about Newton's second law drawn from a textbook should be cited in the references section, with the author, title, publisher and year of publication included.
